active_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.linalg for Kalman filter state-space estimation
active_paradigms.description: Implement a Kalman filter using scipy.linalg for matrix operations. Model the signal as a state-space system with position (signal value) and velocity (trend) states. Use a transition matrix F=[[1,dt],[0,1]] to propagate states, and measurement matrix H=[1,0] to observe position. Tune process noise Q and measurement noise R to balance responsiveness vs. smoothness. The Kalman filter naturally handles non-stationary signals and minimizes lag through predictive state updates. Return filtered position estimates as the output signal. This differs from the previous numpy.linalg attempt by using scipy.linalg for more stable matrix operations and proper state-space formulation.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error and false reversal penalty - Kalman filter predicts signal values rather than just smoothing, reducing lag while maintaining smoothness
active_paradigms.cautions: Ensure proper initialization of state covariance P. Tune Q/R ratio carefully - too much Q causes noise amplification, too little causes lag. Handle edge cases where signal length < window_size.

active_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.butter with scipy.signal.filtfilt for zero-phase Butterworth filtering
active_paradigms.description: Design a Butterworth low-pass filter using scipy.signal.butter with order based on window_size. Apply zero-phase filtering using scipy.signal.filtfilt which filters forward and backward, eliminating phase delay entirely. Set cutoff frequency inversely proportional to window_size to match the smoothing scale. This approach fundamentally differs from Wiener filtering by using frequency-domain design and zero-phase processing. The Butterworth filter provides maximally flat passband response, preserving signal dynamics while attenuating high-frequency noise.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error and tracking accuracy - zero-phase filtering eliminates the lag penalty completely while maintaining good noise reduction
active_paradigms.cautions: Filter order should be moderate (3-5) to avoid edge artifacts. Cutoff frequency must be carefully scaled to window_size. Handle edge effects by extending signal or using appropriate padding.

active_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.firwin with scipy.signal.lfilter for custom FIR filtering
active_paradigms.description: Design a custom FIR low-pass filter using scipy.signal.firwin with a window length matching the processing window. Use a Kaiser window for optimal stopband attenuation. Apply the filter using scipy.signal.lfilter with zero-phase initialization via lfilter_zi. The FIR filter provides linear phase response and precise control over frequency characteristics. Design the filter with a cutoff that balances noise reduction and trend preservation based on the window_size parameter.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes and false reversals - FIR filters with linear phase preserve signal structure better than IIR filters, reducing spurious directional changes
active_paradigms.cautions: FIR filter length affects computational cost and edge effects. Use appropriate window function (Kaiser or Hamming) for good stopband rejection. Ensure filter coefficients sum to 1 for unity gain.

tried_paradigms.idea: Implement Kalman filter with state-space estimation using numpy
tried_paradigms.description: Build a Kalman filter that models the signal as a state-space system with process and measurement noise. The filter uses prediction-correction cycle: predict next state based on previous state and dynamics, then correct using new measurement. This provides optimal estimation for linear Gaussian systems, naturally balancing smoothness and tracking. The Kalman gain automatically adjusts based on estimated noise levels, providing adaptive filtering without fixed weights. Implement with state vector [position, velocity] to capture trend, reducing lag through predictive capability and minimizing false reversals through probabilistic state estimation.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: All metrics simultaneously through optimal Bayesian estimation, especially lag error (L_recent) and tracking accuracy through predictive capability
tried_paradigms.cautions: Initialize covariance matrices properly, tune process and measurement noise parameters, ensure numerical stability with matrix operations

tried_paradigms.description: Replace the Wiener filter with Savitzky-Golay filter which fits a polynomial to each sliding window using least squares. This preserves higher-order signal features like peaks and slopes while smoothing noise. Use window_length=21 (odd, larger than current 20) and polyorder=3 for cubic polynomial fitting. The filter naturally reduces slope changes and false reversals by maintaining signal dynamics. Unlike Wiener which only considers local variance, Savitzky-Golay preserves the shape of the signal better.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes (S), false reversals (R), and tracking accuracy (correlation)
tried_paradigms.cautions: Window length must be odd and greater than polynomial order. Edge effects may occur at signal boundaries. Polyorder=3 is good balance between smoothness and feature preservation.

tried_paradigms.description: Apply exponential smoothing with exponentially decaying weights to recent observations. This minimizes lag error by giving higher weight to recent samples while still smoothing noise. Configure with trend='add' and seasonal=None for non-seasonal signals. The smoothing parameter alpha (typically 0.2-0.4) controls responsiveness vs smoothness tradeoff. This approach adapts better to non-stationary signals than fixed-window filters.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error (L_recent, L_avg) and tracking accuracy
tried_paradigms.cautions: Initial values may cause edge effects. Alpha too high increases noise sensitivity, too low increases lag. Works best for signals with gradual changes rather than abrupt jumps.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use Hampel filter combining scipy.signal.medfilt and scipy.stats.mad for outlier removal
tried_paradigms.description: Implement Hampel filter which detects outliers using median absolute deviation (MAD) and replaces them with local median. First compute local median using medfilt with kernel_size=11, then calculate MAD of residuals. Replace values where |signal - median| > k * MAD (k=3.0 typical) with the local median. This is robust to outliers that create false reversals while preserving genuine signal structure better than simple median filtering.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: False reversals (R) and slope changes (S) by removing noise-induced outliers
tried_paradigms.cautions: Hampel filter is more aggressive on outliers than smoothing filters. May smooth genuine sharp transitions if threshold k is too low. Works best when outliers are sparse relative to signal length.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.medfilt with adaptive window for edge-preserving smoothing
tried_paradigms.description: Replace Wiener filter with scipy.signal.medfilt which uses median-based filtering instead of mean-based. Median filtering is more robust to outliers and preserves signal edges better, directly reducing false reversals and slope changes. Implement adaptive window sizing based on local signal variance - use smaller windows in low-variance regions for responsiveness and larger windows in high-variance regions for noise reduction. The median filter naturally handles the non-stationary characteristics of the test signals better than linear filters. This approach targets the 60% combined penalty from slope changes and false reversals.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes (30% weight) and false reversal penalty (30% weight) by preserving genuine trend changes while filtering noise-induced reversals
tried_paradigms.cautions: Median filter output length may differ from input - ensure proper alignment with evaluator's delay calculation. Window size must be odd. Test different window sizes (5, 7, 9) to find optimal trade-off between smoothness and responsiveness.

tried_paradigms.idea: Implement hysteresis-based trend confirmation to eliminate false reversals
tried_paradigms.description: After initial filtering (using any base filter), apply a hysteresis mechanism that only confirms a trend change after the new direction persists for N consecutive samples. Track the current trend state (up/down/flat) and require sustained evidence before switching states. This directly addresses the false reversal penalty which compares filtered signal trend changes against clean signal. Implement using numpy arrays to count consecutive samples in same direction before confirming a reversal. This post-processing step can be combined with any base filter to reduce R(θ) penalty without affecting other metrics significantly.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: False reversal penalty R(θ) (30% weight) by preventing noise-induced spurious direction changes that don't match the clean signal
tried_paradigms.cautions: Hysteresis threshold N must be tuned carefully - too high causes lag, too low allows false reversals. Typical range 3-7 samples. Must account for the evaluator's delay calculation when aligning filtered signal with clean signal for comparison.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use double exponential smoothing (Holt's method) for better trend tracking
tried_paradigms.description: Implement Holt's double exponential smoothing which tracks both level and trend components separately, providing better responsiveness to genuine signal changes than Wiener filter. Use two smoothing parameters: alpha for level (0.1-0.3) and beta for trend (0.05-0.15). This method naturally reduces lag error while maintaining smoothness, addressing the 40% combined penalty from lag and tracking error. The trend component allows the filter to anticipate direction changes rather than just react to them. Implement using numpy array operations for efficiency.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error (20% weight) and average tracking error (20% weight) by better tracking genuine signal trends while maintaining responsiveness
tried_paradigms.cautions: Two parameters (alpha, beta) need tuning for optimal performance. Different test signals may require different parameter values. Ensure causal implementation (only use past data) for real-time compatibility. Initialize level and trend from first few samples carefully.

tried_paradigms.idea: Implement adaptive Kalman filter with state-space estimation using numpy.linalg
tried_paradigms.description: Build a custom Kalman filter using numpy.linalg.inv for matrix operations that estimates both signal value and velocity (slope). The filter uses a constant velocity state-space model where the state vector contains [value, velocity]. Initialize with adaptive covariance based on local signal variance. Update the measurement noise covariance dynamically based on recent signal volatility (higher noise = more smoothing, lower noise = more tracking). This approach directly addresses the lag error vs false reversal tradeoff by predicting signal movement rather than just smoothing. The Kalman filter's predictive nature reduces lag while the state estimation smooths out spurious reversals.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Lag error (L_recent, L_avg) and false reversal penalty (R) by balancing prediction and smoothing
tried_paradigms.cautions: Ensure matrix operations are numerically stable, handle edge cases at signal boundaries, tune process noise covariance to match signal dynamics, avoid over-smoothing which increases lag error

tried_paradigms.idea: Use scipy.signal.decimate with wavelet-based multi-scale decomposition
tried_paradigms.description: Apply multi-resolution analysis using scipy.signal.decimate combined with custom wavelet-like decomposition to separate signal into multiple frequency bands. Decompose the signal into approximation (low-frequency trend) and detail (high-frequency noise) components across 2-3 scales. Analyze the variance ratio between scales to identify which detail coefficients represent noise vs signal dynamics. Reconstruct the signal by keeping approximation coefficients and selectively preserving detail coefficients that exceed a volatility threshold. This preserves genuine rapid signal changes while removing high-frequency noise that causes false reversals.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: False reversal penalty (R) and slope changes (S) by distinguishing noise from genuine signal dynamics
tried_paradigms.cautions: Choose appropriate decomposition levels to avoid losing signal content, ensure boundary handling doesn't introduce artifacts, threshold selection must balance noise removal vs signal preservation

tried_paradigms.idea: Implement robust Hampel-Savitzky-Golay hybrid filter with adaptive windowing
tried_paradigms.description: Create a two-stage filter combining Hampel outlier detection with Savitzky-Golay polynomial smoothing. First stage: use Hampel filter to identify and correct outliers by comparing each sample to local median and median absolute deviation (MAD). Second stage: apply Savitzky-Golay filter with polynomial order 2 or 3 to smooth the outlier-corrected signal while preserving trend dynamics. Implement adaptive windowing where the Savitzky-Golay window size varies based on local signal volatility (larger window for high variance regions, smaller for stable regions). This hybrid approach handles impulsive noise while maintaining trend accuracy.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Slope changes (S) and false reversal penalty (R) while maintaining low lag error
tried_paradigms.cautions: Hampel filter MAD threshold must be calibrated (typically 3 MAD), Savitzky-Golay window must be odd and less than signal length, adaptive windowing must avoid excessive computational overhead
